text.en: From a point outside a circle we can draw exactly two tangents, and they have a beautiful property: their lengths are equal.

From a point inside a circle there is no tangent. From a point on the circle there is one tangent.
From a point outside the circle there are exactly two tangents.
Theorem two: the lengths of the tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
Proof: join OP, OQ and OR. Triangles OPQ and OPR are right triangles with OQ = OR and a common hypotenuse OP, so they are congruent by RHS.
Hence PQ = PR. The line OP also bisects the angle between the tangents.
Example: tangents PA and PB from P with angle APB = 80 degrees. Then angle OAP = 90 and angle AOB = 100.
In a circle touching all sides of a quadrilateral, the sum of the opposite sides is equal: AB + CD = AD + BC.
Use equal tangents to set up equations in lengths and angles.

problem.en: Two tangents PA and PB are drawn from P to a circle with centre O. If angle APB = 70 degrees, find angle AOB.

text.en: OA and OB are perpendicular to PA and PB, so angle OAP = angle OBP = 90.

prompt.en: State the theorem about tangents from an external point.

commonMisconceptions.en: Believing tangents from a point can be unequal

points.en: From an external point, two tangents can be drawn and they are equal in length.
The line joining the point to the centre bisects the angle between them.
In a quadrilateral around a circle, sums of opposite sides are equal.
